name: Role & RoleBinding basics
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration. Drill EVERY RBAC corner harder than the exam: namespaced Role vs cluster-scoped ClusterRole, binding to users and ServiceAccounts, reusing a ClusterRole inside one namespace via a RoleBinding, least-privilege with resourceNames, apiGroups for subresources, approving a CSR, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Role + RoleBinding (namespaced)
questions.teach:
**RBAC** decides who can do what. A **Role** lists allowed *verbs* on *resources* inside one namespace; a **RoleBinding** grants that Role to a subject (here user `dev`). Build both with `kubectl create role` / `kubectl create rolebinding`.

**Gotcha:** a Role alone grants nothing — access only exists once a RoleBinding points a subject at it.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `rbac-learn`, create a Role `pod-reader` allowing `get,list,watch` on `pods`, and a RoleBinding `dev-pr` granting it to user `dev`.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n rbac-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods`, then `kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-pr --role=pod-reader --user=dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-pr --role=pod-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn   # -> yes

verification.description: Role pod-reader (get,list,watch pods) bound to user dev; dev can list pods but not delete

questions.eli5:
Think of your cluster as a big office building, and RBAC as the security desk that decides who gets to do what.

Two separate things have to line up:

- A **Role** is a *job description* pinned to the wall of one room (one namespace). It says what actions are allowed — like "may **get, list, watch** the pods" — but it has nobody's name on it. By itself it does **nothing**; it's just a piece of paper describing a job.
- A **RoleBinding** is the *hire letter* that staples a person (the user `dev`) to that job description. Only once the staple exists does `dev` actually get those powers — and only inside that one room.

So the recipe is always two steps: write the job description (`kubectl create role`), then hand it to someone (`kubectl create rolebinding`).

To check whether it worked, you ask the security desk directly: `kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn`. It answers plain `yes` or `no`.

**Watch out for:**

- A **Role alone grants nothing** — no RoleBinding, no access. This is the #1 trap.
- A Role/RoleBinding is **namespaced**: it only works in the one namespace you created it in. Forget `-n` and you may build it in the wrong room.
- RBAC is **additive and allow-only** — there are no "deny" rules. Whatever no rule grants is denied by default.
- Verbs are exact strings: `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`, `delete`. `read` is not a verb.
- `list` and `get` are different powers — granting one doesn't grant the other.
questions.deepDive:
## Role + RoleBinding (namespaced RBAC) — full rundown

### The one-sentence model
**A Role describes permissions; a RoleBinding grants them to a subject.** Neither does anything alone — access exists only when a binding connects a *subject* to a *role* inside a namespace. RBAC is **purely additive** (allow-only): there is no "deny" rule, and anything not explicitly allowed is denied.

### The four RBAC objects
| Object | Scope | Holds rules? | Grants to subjects? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Role** | one namespace | ✅ verbs on resources | ❌ |
| **ClusterRole** | cluster-wide | ✅ (incl. cluster-scoped resources) | ❌ |
| **RoleBinding** | one namespace | ❌ | ✅ (to a Role *or* ClusterRole) |
| **ClusterRoleBinding** | cluster-wide | ❌ | ✅ (to a ClusterRole only) |

### Anatomy of a rule
Every rule in a Role answers three questions: **verbs** (what actions), **apiGroups** (which API), **resources** (on what).
```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]          # "" = the core group (pods, services, configmaps, secrets...)
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
```
- `apiGroups: [""]` is the **core/legacy** group — pods, services, endpoints, configmaps, secrets, nodes, namespaces, PVs/PVCs.
- Other groups: `apps` (deployments, replicasets, daemonsets, statefulsets), `batch` (jobs, cronjobs), `rbac.authorization.k8s.io` (roles, rolebindings), `networking.k8s.io` (ingresses, networkpolicies).

### The verbs
| Verb | Meaning | resourceNames-restrictable? |
|---|---|---|
| `get` | read one named object | ✅ |
| `list` | enumerate the collection | ❌ |
| `watch` | stream changes | ❌ |
| `create` | make a new object | ❌ |
| `update` | replace an object | ✅ |
| `patch` | partially modify | ✅ |
| `delete` | remove one object | ✅ |
| `deletecollection` | bulk delete | ❌ |
| `*` | all verbs | — |

### Imperative commands (fast on the exam)
```bash
# Role: verbs + resources, inside a namespace
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role pod-reader \
  --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods

# RoleBinding: bind the Role to a subject
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-pr \
  --role=pod-reader --user=dev

# other subject flags:
#   --user=<name>              a (human) user
#   --group=<name>             a group
#   --serviceaccount=<ns>:<sa> a ServiceAccount (note the colon)
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-reader
  namespace: rbac-learn
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get","list","watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-pr
  namespace: rbac-learn
roleRef:                               # which role (immutable!)
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
subjects:                              # who gets it
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: User
  name: dev
```

### Testing access — `kubectl auth can-i`
```bash
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn      # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn    # -> no
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev -n rbac-learn         # dump all perms
```
`--as=<user>` impersonates a subject (needs impersonate privilege, which cluster-admin has). `--as-group=` impersonates a group.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Role without a RoleBinding grants nothing.** The binding is what activates it.
- **Role/RoleBinding are namespaced.** Omitting `-n` puts them in `default`. Access is confined to that one namespace.
- `roleRef` is **immutable** — to point a binding at a different role you must **delete and recreate** it.
- `list` ≠ `get`. A rule with only `get` won't let `kubectl get pods` (which lists) succeed.
- The subject name in a binding is **not validated** — binding to user `dve` (typo) or a nonexistent SA silently grants nothing.
- RBAC is **allow-only**; you cannot write a rule that denies. Remove the grant instead.
- Users/groups aren't objects in Kubernetes — they come from your auth layer (certs, OIDC). You bind to the *name* regardless.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n rbac-learn create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n rbac-learn create rolebinding dev-pr --role=pod-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=dev -n rbac-learn      # yes
```

questions.title: ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped)
questions.teach:
Cluster-scoped resources like **nodes** live outside any namespace, so a namespaced Role can't reach them. Use a **ClusterRole** for the rules and a **ClusterRoleBinding** to grant them cluster-wide.

**Gotcha:** check cluster-scoped access with **no** `-n` flag — `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev`.
questions.prompt:
Create a ClusterRole `node-reader` allowing `get,list` on `nodes`, and a ClusterRoleBinding `dev-nr` granting it to user `dev`.

Target: `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev` → `yes`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes`, then `kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev   # -> yes

verification.description: ClusterRole node-reader (get,list nodes) bound cluster-wide to dev; can list nodes but not list secrets

questions.eli5:
Some things in a cluster live *inside* rooms (namespaces) — like pods and configmaps. But other things belong to the **whole building** and aren't in any room at all: **nodes** are a great example. There's no "which room is this node in?" — it just *is*, cluster-wide.

A plain **Role** is a job description pinned inside one room, so it can only talk about things in that room. It literally cannot describe a permission on a node, because nodes aren't in any room. That's where **ClusterRole** comes in: it's a job description that applies to the *entire building*, so it can cover building-wide things like nodes.

To hand that building-wide job to someone everywhere, you use a **ClusterRoleBinding** — the hire letter that works across the whole building.

So for nodes: `ClusterRole` for the rules, `ClusterRoleBinding` to grant it, and now `dev` can list nodes anywhere.

When you check it, there's a twist: because the permission isn't tied to any room, you ask **without** naming a room — no `-n` flag: `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev`.

**Watch out for:**

- **Cluster-scoped resources need a ClusterRole** — a namespaced Role simply can't grant access to nodes, namespaces, PVs, etc.
- **Check with no `-n` flag.** Adding `-n something` for a cluster-scoped resource asks the wrong question and can confuse you.
- A **ClusterRoleBinding grants the powers everywhere** — in *every* namespace and on cluster-scoped objects. That's powerful; don't over-grant.
- A ClusterRole is still just a job description — without a binding it grants nothing.
- Same ClusterRole, bound two ways: a **ClusterRoleBinding** = cluster-wide; a **RoleBinding** = only that one namespace (that's a different lesson).
questions.deepDive:
## ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped RBAC) — full rundown

### The mental model
Resources are either **namespaced** (pods, configmaps, deployments — they live inside a namespace) or **cluster-scoped** (nodes, namespaces, persistentvolumes, clusterroles). A namespaced **Role** can only grant permissions on namespaced resources *in its own namespace*. To grant access to **cluster-scoped** resources, you need a **ClusterRole**, and to grant it cluster-wide you need a **ClusterRoleBinding**.

### Namespaced vs cluster-scoped resources
| Cluster-scoped (need ClusterRole) | Namespaced (Role is enough) |
|---|---|
| `nodes` | `pods`, `services`, `configmaps`, `secrets` |
| `namespaces` | `deployments`, `replicasets`, `statefulsets` |
| `persistentvolumes` | `jobs`, `cronjobs` |
| `clusterroles`, `clusterrolebindings` | `roles`, `rolebindings` |
| `storageclasses`, `csinodes` | `persistentvolumeclaims`, `endpoints` |

```bash
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false   # the cluster-scoped list
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true    # the namespaced list
```

### The binding matrix (what grants what)
| Binding | References | Grant scope |
|---|---|---|
| **ClusterRoleBinding** → ClusterRole | ClusterRole only | **cluster-wide** (all namespaces + cluster-scoped resources) |
| **RoleBinding** → ClusterRole | ClusterRole | that **one namespace** only (namespaced resources) |
| **RoleBinding** → Role | Role (same ns) | that one namespace |
| ClusterRoleBinding → Role | ❌ invalid | — |

Key fact: a ClusterRoleBinding to `node-reader` lets `dev` read nodes **cluster-wide**, because nodes aren't in any namespace.

### Imperative commands
```bash
# ClusterRole with rules (NO namespace)
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader \
  --verb=get,list --resource=nodes

# ClusterRoleBinding to grant it cluster-wide
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr \
  --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev
```

### Equivalent YAML
```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader          # no namespace field
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes"]
  verbs: ["get","list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-nr
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-reader
subjects:
- apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: User
  name: dev
```

### Testing cluster-scoped access
```bash
# NO -n for cluster-scoped resources:
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev           # -> yes
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=dev         # -> no (not granted)
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=dev               # everything dev can do cluster-wide
```

### Built-in ClusterRoles worth knowing
Kubernetes ships default (aggregated) ClusterRoles you can bind directly:
| ClusterRole | Grants |
|---|---|
| `cluster-admin` | everything (superuser) — bind via ClusterRoleBinding |
| `admin` | full RW within a namespace (typically via RoleBinding) |
| `edit` | RW on most objects in a namespace, no RBAC |
| `view` | read-only in a namespace, no secrets |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Namespaced Role can't reach cluster-scoped resources** (nodes, PVs, namespaces). Use a ClusterRole.
- **Test cluster-scoped access without `-n`.** `kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev -n foo` asks the wrong question.
- A **ClusterRoleBinding is global** — the subject gets the ClusterRole's permissions in *every* namespace and on cluster-scoped objects. Over-granting here is a common security slip.
- A **ClusterRoleBinding cannot reference a Role** — only a ClusterRole.
- ClusterRole still needs a binding; rules alone grant nothing.
- To scope a ClusterRole's rules to a single namespace, bind it with a **RoleBinding** instead (separate technique).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl create clusterrole node-reader --verb=get,list --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding dev-nr --clusterrole=node-reader --user=dev
kubectl auth can-i list nodes --as=dev           # yes  (no -n!)
```
